_doc: Search performance budgets. `budgets` is the MEASURED record (npm run perf:search, live production data) and is documentation a human reads. `static` is the machine-enforced half: scripts/check-search-perf-budget.mjs (npm run ci:search-perf-budget) runs inside the secret-less ci:gates chain, so it cannot time a query — it enforces the structural invariants that keep the measured numbers true (ISR revalidate, fetch timeouts, cache wrappers, row caps, bounded reads). Refresh `budgets` with: npm run perf:search -- --json

measurement.environment: laptop over the public internet to Supabase project dwvlophlbvvygjfxcrhm, live production data. Vercel runs closer to the database, so production is faster than these numbers, never slower.
measurement.cacheNote: The measurement stubs next/cache so unstable_cache is a passthrough. Every timed call is a real query. 'cold' is the first run, 'warm' the median of the rest — a warm DATABASE, not a warm Next cache.
measurement.budgetRule: budgetMs is set at roughly 2x the worst observed cold time with a 500 ms floor, so network jitter and a cold Postgres buffer never trip it while a real regression (dropped index, lost cache wrapper, unbounded select) shows up as a multiple.

budgets.why: Whole-MV first page. The slowest unfiltered read, because no index narrows it before the sort.
The single most common search shape on the site. Indexed city read plus an exact count in one query.
City plus price plus beds. Adding registry filters must not cost more than the city read itself.
Ten filters across price, beds, baths, sqft, year, garage, acreage and two feature booleans, sorted by price. The all-filters sheet's worst realistic case.
PostGIS key resolution plus chunked .in() re-read. Two round trips by construction, so it carries the widest budget of the row paths.
Head count behind the live match total. Runs on every filter change, so it has to stay under a quarter second.
Same head count with seven predicates. The count must not diverge from the row read it labels.
3,808 facet rows paged out of search_facet_counts at 1,000 per page. Four round trips, cached for 15 minutes to match the table's refresh.
The shapes RPC on its own, one Bend-sized polygon returning 620 keys. Budget matches the drawn-shape row path it feeds.

The RPC fallback: a closed (sold) scope plus a jsonb-derived feature filter, the combination that falls out of listing_search_mv and into search_listings_advanced. This line was the single degraded path in this file until 2026-08-01, when it returned rows 0 and error 57014 for every anonymous visitor. Budget is roughly 2x the measured cold (worst cold across two runs was 5877 ms under a concurrent MV refresh) and sits deliberately just under the function's own 12 s statement_timeout, which is the hard ceiling: a regression that slows the path without erroring outright still trips this budget.

knownDegraded.shape: viewContains preset, no city (the five view SEO pages)
knownDegraded.status: STILL DEGRADED at the production 12s ceiling. The TOAST cause is closed and the results are now correct, but the shape is still too slow to complete.
knownDegraded.shapes: Measured through the DAL (getListingsWithAdvanced, a real top-level PostgREST call, so the function's own 12s statement_timeout is armed): mountain-view 12,153 ms 57014 degraded; river-view 12,167 ms 57014 degraded; golf-course-view 12,118 ms 57014 degraded; lake-view 12,068 ms 57014 degraded; water-view 11,021 ms completes, degraded=false, 0 rows for a content reason (below). Run-to-run it flickers — river-view completed on one run and timed out on the next — which is what sitting on the ceiling looks like.
knownDegraded.whatWasFixed: p_view_contains was the last predicate reading listings.details. Migrations 20260801020000 / 021000 / 030000 projected details->>'View' into listing_feature_flags.view_text (trigger-maintained, 594,196-row sharded backfill, pg_trgm GIN index) and repointed the RPC at it, so the shape no longer detoasts a ~10 KB jsonb document per candidate row. Under a relaxed timeout the shapes now COMPLETE and return CORRECT rows (Mountain 2,877 matches, River 282, Golf 280, Lake 222, Water 0), where before the fix they could only ever return 57014 and zero rows. That is real progress and it is a precondition for the routing fix below, but on its own it does not get these pages under the ceiling.
knownDegraded.remainingRootCause: A JOIN-ORDER problem driven by an unindexable predicate, the same open class already documented for p_keywords. 'Active' is expressed as "StandardStatus" ILIKE '%Active%', which no index can serve, and these five pages set NO city, so there is no cheap narrowing predicate anywhere in the shape. Both join orders were measured and both lose: driving from the trgm index does 198,768 flag matches nested-looped into listings (14.4 s of a 16.3 s plan), and forcing a hash semi-join instead pays a 9.6 s Parallel Seq Scan of listings to find the 7,742 active rows (11.0 s total). The residual cost is the seq scan, not the projection.
knownDegraded.correctNextStep: Route these presets to the listing_search_mv fast path rather than to this RPC. The MV IS the indexable on-market projection the shape needs, and it already carries a view_types array column. That is a routing change in hasAdvancedFilters() (app/actions/listings.ts) plus an index on view_types, and it MUST be preceded by an equivalence proof between view_types and details->>'View' — the flat promoted columns on listings have twice been found to disagree materially with the jsonb (see 20260731210000), so this is exactly the trap to check for before switching.
knownDegraded.notAPerfIssue: /homes-for-sale/water-view renders empty for a content reason, not a performance one: no active listing's View field contains the string 'Water'. Verified both expressions over the whole active population — old details->>'View' ILIKE '%Water%' = 0, new view_text ILIKE '%Water%' = 0. It would render empty against an infinitely fast query.
knownDegraded.projectionCorrectness: view_text vs details->>'View': 0 mismatches over 16,531 rows (the entire 7,742-row active population plus an 8,789-row 1.5% block sample across all 8 statuses), exact 594,196 = 594,196 coverage with 0 listings lacking a flags row, and per-term equality over the active population (Mountain 2877/2877, River 282/282, Golf 280/280, Lake 222/222, Water 0/0). Two RPC parity shapes fingerprinted identically before and after the swap.
knownDegraded.doNotMisreadWarmNumbers: Timing these five inside ONE transaction reports 4.3-14.6 s and looks much better than reality, because the sequential runs share Postgres buffer cache and the function's proconfig statement_timeout does not re-arm inside a larger statement. The DAL numbers above are the ones that describe production. This trap cost a wrong reading once already on 2026-08-01.

timeoutCeilings.name: withTimeout
timeoutCeilings.why: The split view degrades to an empty result rather than blocking the render on a slow Supabase.

timeoutCeilings.name: withTimeout
timeoutCeilings.why: Secondary fetches on the SEO search routes fail soft fast.

timeoutCeilings.name: LISTINGS_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS
timeoutCeilings.why: Ceiling for the primary listings fetch. Raising it means a user waits longer on the known-degraded RPC path.

rowCaps.name: SHAPE_KEY_PAGE
rowCaps.why: One PostgREST page. Above 1,000 the response silently truncates.

rowCaps.name: MAX_SHAPE_KEYS
rowCaps.why: Ceiling on key resolution before the search degrades to the bbox fallback. Each 1,000 keys is another round trip.

rowCaps.name: SHAPE_KEY_CHUNK
rowCaps.why: Keys per .in() chunk. Larger chunks push the request URL past safe length.

rowCaps.name: PAGE_SIZE
rowCaps.why: Facet paging step, pinned to the PostgREST cap.

rowCaps.name: cap
rowCaps.why: Viewport row cap behind the map. Every row is a marker plus a card, so this is a render budget as much as a query budget.

rowCaps.name: limit
rowCaps.why: The filter schema's page-size ceiling. Above the PostgREST cap the read truncates without an error.

resolved.status: CLOSED. Moved out of knownDegraded into budgets on 2026-08-01.
resolved.rootCause: ROW-LEVEL SECURITY plus a non-LEAKPROOF operator. public.listings has RLS enabled and the anon policy is one predicate, lower(coalesce("StandardStatus",'')) NOT LIKE 'coming%soon%'. PostgreSQL will not evaluate a non-leakproof user qual ahead of a security qual, and pg_catalog.texticlike (ILIKE) has proleakproof = false, so for anon the planner could not use idx_listings_city_trgm for "City" ILIKE $1 and fell back to a Parallel Seq Scan of the ~13 GB listings relation. Pre-existing and not feature-specific: closed+Bend with NO advanced filter measured 21,822 ms as anon against 885 ms as postgres.
resolved.fix: Migration 20260801010000 made search_listings_advanced SECURITY DEFINER with a pinned search_path, and wrote the Coming Soon exclusion into the body explicitly and unconditionally (three places: the base CTE, the exclude-sold-since subquery, and the projection join). The function no longer fights RLS, so the planner is free to use the indexes; the visible result set for an anonymous caller is unchanged because the same predicate excludes the same rows. EXECUTE was revoked from PUBLIC and granted to exactly anon, authenticated and service_role.
resolved.rejected: Marking texticlike/texticnlike LEAKPROOF was rejected by the broker: one catalog change would fix every RLS-protected ILIKE in the database but it is a database-wide security-posture decision, and it is not worth making to speed up one function. Rewriting "City" ILIKE as a leakproof equality was rejected because ILIKE 'Bend' also matches 'BEND', lower() is itself not leakproof, and MLS city casing is not canonical.
resolved.proof: PLANS, same query text, as anon vs with the explicit predicate and no RLS: Parallel Seq Scan on listings, 4,949 ms of a 5,103 ms plan, 165,986 buffers -> Bitmap Index Scan on idx_listings_city_trgm with Index Cond ("City" ~~* 'Bend'), 1,157 ms, 87,256 buffers. TIMING as anon, before vs after, same arguments: bend closed plain 11,127 -> 1,422 ms; bend closed + hasView 11,532 -> 1,201 ms; redmond closed price band 5,377 -> 1,072 ms; multi-city closed 1,346 -> 656 ms (smallest gain because = ANY is leakproof and was never blocked, which independently confirms the mechanism). PARITY: 12 argument shapes run AS ANON with both the pre-change clone and the new function inside ONE statement, so both share a single snapshot and MLS drift cannot produce a false mismatch; md5 over row order, ListNumber, ListingKey, ListPrice, StandardStatus, ModificationTimestamp and the full details document, plus full_count, identical on all 12.
resolved.comingSoonContainment: The function bypasses RLS, so the exclusion is now the function's own responsibility. Verified as anon across 7 shapes chosen to select FOR Coming Soon rows (Bend all-status 13 baited rows, the exact Coming Soon price band, Redmond 2, Sunriver 2, status=NULL, status=coming_soon, and all 16 cities that hold one, 38 baited rows): zero leaked. Verified again synthetically as POSTGRES, which is subject to no RLS backstop at all so a leak could not be masked: a real Bend listing was flipped to each of 'Coming Soon', 'coming soon', 'COMING SOON', 'Coming-Soon' and 'ComingSoon' inside a subtransaction, control before the flip returned it (1), every spelling returned 0, and the subtransaction was force-rolled-back.
